common_name: China Pink Azalea (Deep Salmon-Pink Southern Indica Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; China Pink is a classic Southern Indica azalea valued for deep salmon-pink spring flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade, mulching well to protect the shallow, fibrous root system common to all azaleas. China Pink is a classic Southern Indica-type azalea bearing large, funnel-shaped flowers in a deep, warm salmon-pink, opening in a heavy spring flush on a large, vigorous, mounding evergreen shrub typical of the Indica group. Its bold color and generous bloom size have made it a long-standing favorite for Southern foundation plantings and mass displays, often combined with white or red azalea cultivars for a traditional layered spring show. Water deeply during dry spells, especially in the first year or two after planting, and prune lightly right after flowering, since next year's buds form soon after the spring bloom ends.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Azalea Cultivars for the Landscape
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Azaleas for Texas Gardens

common_name: Girard's Rose Azalea (Compact Rose-Pink Girard Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5-5.5) soil in partial shade; Girard's Rose is a compact Girard hybrid azalea valued for reliable rose-pink spring bloom and cold hardiness.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic soil in partial shade. Girard's Rose is a compact hybrid azalea from the Girard breeding program in Ohio, developed to combine good cold hardiness with the dense, fine-textured, small-leaf habit typical of Kurume-type azaleas, producing a heavy flush of bright rose-pink single flowers each spring on a tight, mounding evergreen shrub. Its cold tolerance extends its usefulness into cooler parts of the azalea-growing range than many Southern Indica cultivars, while its dense, compact habit needs little pruning to maintain a neat, formal shape. Water deeply during dry spells and mulch well to protect the shallow root system, and prune, if needed, right after flowering to avoid removing the next season's buds.
